tasks.name: Boiling Eggs
facts: Older eggs peel easier because the membrane separates from the shell as it ages over time.
A perfectly boiled egg has layers: whites set at 60°C and yolk at 65°C—timing is everything!
The sulfur smell in overcooked eggs happens when hydrogen sulfide forms—don't overcook!
Adding salt to boiling water raises the boiling point, helping eggs cook faster.
An egg's shell is porous and contains about 17,000 tiny pores that allow gases to escape.
The chicken's diet affects egg yolk color—marigolds and algae make them more golden.
Eggs cooled immediately after boiling stop cooking and peel more easily.
A fresh egg sinks in water while an old egg floats due to the air cell inside.
Room-temperature eggs crack less when boiling than cold eggs from the fridge.
Eggshells are made of calcium carbonate, the same stuff as chalk and limestone.

tasks.name: Heating Milk
facts: Heating milk to 65°C denatures proteins and creates a thicker skin on top, loved in many recipes.
Milk scorches at 71°C—just below boiling—so watch carefully to avoid burnt edges.
The lactose in milk becomes sweeter when heated, making warm milk taste naturally sweeter.
Cow's milk is about 88% water and 3.5% protein—the exact composition of comfort.
Milk proteins called casein curdle when heated with acidic ingredients like lemon juice.
Whole milk creates a richer foam for lattes because fat content stabilizes bubbles.
Ancient civilizations boiled milk to preserve it, discovering pasteurization centuries early.
Milk has a natural enzyme called lipase that breaks down fat and creates 'tangy' flavors.
Adding milk to hot tea prevents tannins from staining your teeth.
Plant-based milks require less heat to warm but don't develop the same creamy texture.

tasks.name: Cooking Rice
facts: The absorption method works because each grain absorbs exactly the right amount of water.
White rice is 'polished' while brown rice keeps the bran—making brown take longer to cook.
Rice cookers work by detecting steam changes when all water is absorbed—pure engineering!
Rinsing rice removes excess starch that makes it gluey, creating fluffier grains.
Basmati rice has an interlocking protein structure that makes it stay separate when cooked.
Rice is the staple food for over 3.5 billion people—more than any other grain.
Arborio rice has high starch content, perfect for risotto because it releases creamy texture.
Aging rice for 2+ years makes it fluffier because moisture slowly evaporates from grains.
Covering rice while cooking traps steam and ensures even heat distribution.
Left-over rice must be cooled quickly and refrigerated to prevent bacterial growth.

tasks.name: Water Motor
facts: Water is the only substance that exists naturally in all three states on Earth.
A liter of water weighs exactly 1 kilogram—so 20L equals 20kg of weight!
Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, which is why water can climb up plant roots.
Stored water can develop bacteria if not covered—keep tanks sealed for safety.
Room-temperature water (20-25°C) is optimal for most household uses and plants.
Pumps work by creating pressure differences that move water against gravity.
Soft water (low minerals) flows easier through pipes than hard water (high minerals).
Ancient Romans built aqueducts using gravity and mathematics—no pumps needed!
A dripping faucet wastes 3,000 gallons per year—fix leaks immediately.
Boiling water for 20 minutes kills most bacteria, making it safe to drink.

tasks.name: Brewing Tea
facts: Green tea steeps best at 70-80°C; boiling water destroys delicate flavors and antioxidants.
Black tea oxidation gives it color—it's processed differently but from the same plant as green!
Herbal infusions aren't technically 'tea' unless they contain leaves from Camellia sinensis plant.
Tea's caffeine content depends on steep time—5 minutes gives more caffeine than 1 minute.
The tannic acid in tea reduces iron absorption, so avoid tea with iron-rich meals.
Quality tea leaves unfurl beautifully when steeped, releasing maximum flavor and aroma.
Tea originated in China 5,000 years ago when leaves accidentally blew into a pot of water!
Oversteeping tea makes it bitter because tannins extract too much from the leaves.
Loose leaf tea has more surface area than tea bags, brewing faster and tasting fresher.
Adding milk to tea prevents tannins from staining teeth and smooths bitter flavors.

tasks.name: Steaming Vegetables
facts: Steaming preserves more vitamins than boiling because vegetables don't leach into water.
Broccoli's sulforaphane (anti-cancer compound) is strongest when lightly steamed, not raw.
Carrots become sweeter when steamed because heat breaks down cell walls, releasing sugars.
Steam temperature is lower than boiling water (95-100°C vs 100°C), protecting delicate vitamins.
Frozen vegetables steam perfectly fine and sometimes retain more nutrients than fresh.
Steaming time varies: broccoli needs 4 minutes, carrots need 8 minutes—don't mix!
Over-steaming vegetables creates a sulfurous smell from hydrogen sulfide gas release.
Steamed vegetables maintain bright color because chlorophyll isn't destroyed by acid.
Adding a pinch of salt to steam water seasons vegetables from within as they cook.
Vegetables can be steamed ahead and reheated without losing texture or nutrients.

tasks.name: Cooking Pasta
facts: Al dente (firm bite) originated in Italy and preserves better digestion than mushy pasta.
Pasta water's starch helps sauce stick to noodles—don't drain it all away!
Adding salt to pasta water is essential; it flavors the pasta, not just the water.
Freshly boiled pasta cools quickly when sauced but cooked pasta stays warm longer.
Dried pasta (durum wheat) is different from fresh pasta (soft wheat)—cook times vary greatly.
Pasta triples in weight when cooked because it absorbs water through its porous structure.
Stirring pasta in the first minute prevents sticking; after that, it won't stick together.
Whole wheat pasta takes 2-3 minutes longer than refined pasta due to higher fiber density.
Gluten network development makes pasta chewy—it's not just about cooking time.
Shocking pasta in ice water stops cooking immediately, perfect for cold salads.

tasks.name: Laundry Washing
facts: Hot water opens fabric fibers, allowing detergent to penetrate deeper and clean better.
Delicate cycles use less agitation, protecting elastic and intricate stitching from damage.
Washing clothes in cold water saves 90% of energy while still getting them clean.
Detergent molecules have a water-loving and oil-loving end, trapping dirt particles.
Overloading a washing machine prevents proper water circulation and incomplete cleaning.
Modern detergents work in cold water; older ones needed heat to activate fully.
Fabric softeners coat fibers with wax, reducing absorbency and damaging athletic wear.
Leaving wet clothes in the washer creates mildew and musty smells within 24 hours.
Different fabrics need different cycles: denim survives heavy cycle, silk needs gentle.
Sorting by color prevents dye transfer; new dark items bleed color in first few washes.

tasks.name: Meditation & Break
facts: Just 5 minutes of meditation lowers cortisol (stress hormone) and calms the nervous system.
Deep breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system, the body's 'rest mode'.
Regular meditation increases gray matter in the brain region responsible for attention.
A 10-minute break boosts productivity more than working through fatigue without stopping.
Meditation dates back 5,000 years to ancient India and was refined by Buddhist monks.
The 'runner's high' and meditative state both trigger endorphin release in the brain.
Mindfulness meditation reduces blood pressure, heart rate, and muscle tension measurably.
Taking breaks prevents decision fatigue—your brain needs rest to make good choices.
Even 15-minute meditation sessions improve sleep quality and reduce insomnia symptoms.
Meditation rewires the amygdala (fear center), making anxiety less intense over time.

tasks.name: Dishwashing
facts: Hot water breaks down grease better than cold because heat increases molecular movement.
Dish soap is an amphiphilic molecule—it has both water-loving and grease-loving ends.
Pre-soaking dishes loosens dried food, reducing scrubbing time and water consumption.
Hard water (minerals like calcium) leaves spots on dishes even after drying completely.
Drying dishes immediately prevents water spots and bacteria growth from sitting wet.
Vinegar's acidity cuts through grease and mineral deposits better than soap alone.
Scrubbing patterns (circular vs back-and-forth) don't matter—consistent pressure does.
Hot soapy water kills bacteria faster than cold water, making dishes safer.
Air-drying dishes in a rack is more hygienic than towel-drying which spreads bacteria.
Letting dishes air-dry on racks reduces energy use compared to dishwasher heating cycles.
